paragraphs: The next subject that demands our attention is how the executive department of the proposed government is constituted.
Hardly any part of the system could have been harder to arrange than this one. And hardly any part has been attacked with so little fairness or criticized with so little judgment.

Here the writers against the Constitution seem to have made a point of displaying their talent for misrepresentation. Counting on the people's dislike of monarchy, they have tried to recruit all of the public's jealousies and fears against the intended President of the United States. They present him not merely as the embryo of that detested parent but as its full-grown offspring. To prove the supposed family resemblance, they have not hesitated to borrow even from the world of fiction. The powers of a chief executive, in a few respects greater and in others less than those of the governor of New York, have been blown up into more than royal prerogatives. He has been dressed in attributes that surpass in dignity and splendor those of a king of Great Britain. We have been shown him with the diadem sparkling on his brow and the imperial purple trailing behind him. We have seen him on a throne, surrounded by favorites and mistresses, receiving the envoys of foreign rulers with all the haughty pomp of majesty. The images of Asiatic despotism and sensual indulgence have scarcely been left out to crown this exaggerated scene. We have been taught to tremble at the terrifying faces of murderous janizaries and to blush at the unveiled mysteries of a future seraglio.

Attempts this extravagant to disfigure the object, or rather, one might say, to turn it into something else, make it necessary to look carefully at its real nature and form. We need to establish its true appearance, and we need as well to unmask the dishonesty and expose the falsity of the counterfeit likenesses that have been spread so cunningly and so busily.

In doing this, no one could easily look with moderation, or treat seriously, the devices, no less weak than wicked, that have been contrived to twist public opinion on the subject. They go so far beyond the usual license of party trickery, unjustifiable as that is, that even the most fair-minded and tolerant person must set aside the views that incline him to a generous reading of his political adversaries' conduct, and give way to open and unreserved indignation. It is impossible not to charge deliberate imposture and deceit against the gross pretense that a king of Great Britain resembles an executive of the character marked out for the President of the United States. It is still more impossible to withhold that charge from the rash and barefaced expedients used to make the imposition succeed.

I cite one instance as a sample of the general spirit. Here the recklessness has gone so far as to give the President of the United States a power that the proposed instrument EXPRESSLY assigns to the Executives of the individual States. I mean the power of filling casual vacancies in the Senate.

This bold experiment on the discernment of his countrymen was tried by a writer who (whatever his real merit may be) has had no small share of his party's applause,(1) and who has built a whole series of observations on this false and groundless claim, themselves equally false and groundless. Let him now be confronted with the evidence, and let him, if he can, justify or excuse the shameful outrage he has committed against the dictates of truth and the rules of fair dealing.

The second clause of the second section of the second article empowers the President of the United States "to nominate, and by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, judges of the Supreme Court, and all other OFFICERS of United States whose appointments are NOT in the Constitution OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR, and WHICH SHALL BE ESTABLISHED BY LAW." Right after this clause comes another in these words: "The President shall have power to fill up all VACANCIES that may happen DURING THE RECESS OF THE SENATE, by granting commissions which shall EXPIRE AT THE END OF THEIR NEXT SESSION." It is from this last provision that the alleged power of the President to fill vacancies in the Senate has been drawn. Only a little attention to how the clauses connect, and to the plain meaning of their terms, is needed to see that the deduction does not even look valid.

The first of these two clauses, it is plain, merely supplies a way of appointing officers "whose appointments are NOT OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR in the Constitution, and which SHALL BE ESTABLISHED BY LAW." It cannot, of course, reach the appointment of senators. Their appointments are OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR in the Constitution,(2) they are ESTABLISHED BY THE CONSTITUTION, and they will not need to be established later by law. Hardly anyone will dispute this.

The last of these two clauses, it is equally plain, cannot be read to cover the filling of vacancies in the Senate, for the following reasons. First. The way that clause stands in relation to the other, which gives the general method of appointing officers of the United States, shows that it is only a supplement, establishing an auxiliary method of appointment for cases the general method could not handle. The ordinary power of appointment belongs to the President and Senate JOINTLY, and so can be used only while the Senate is in session. But it would have been improper to require this body to sit continuously just to make appointments, and vacancies might arise IN THEIR RECESS that the public service could require to be filled without delay. The next clause is evidently meant to authorize the President, SINGLY, to make temporary appointments "during the recess of the Senate, by granting commissions which shall expire at the end of their next session." Second. If this clause is a supplement to the one before it, then the VACANCIES it mentions must be understood to concern the "officers" described in that preceding clause; and we have seen that its description leaves out the members of the Senate. Third. The period in which the power is to operate, "during the recess of the Senate," and the length of the appointments, "to the end of the next session" of that body, both point toward the meaning of the provision. Had senators been intended, the clause would naturally have tied the temporary power to the recess of the State legislatures, which make the permanent appointments, and not to the recess of the national Senate, which has no part in those appointments. It would also have let the temporary senators serve until the next session of the legislature of the State whose representation had the vacancy, instead of having them expire at the end of the next session of the national Senate. The situation of the body that makes the permanent appointments would naturally have shaped any power over temporary ones. But the national Senate is the only body whose situation the clause takes into account, and so the vacancies it refers to can only be those among officers in whose appointment that body shares authority with the President. Finally, the first and second clauses of the third section of the first article not only remove every possibility of doubt but destroy any pretext of misunderstanding. The first provides that "the Senate of the United States shall be composed of two Senators from each State, chosen BY THE LEGISLATURE THEREOF for six years"; and the second directs that "if vacancies in that body should happen by resignation or otherwise, DURING THE RECESS OF THE LEGISLATURE OF ANY STATE, the Executive THEREOF may make temporary appointments until the NEXT MEETING OF THE LEGISLATURE, which shall then fill such vacancies." Here, in clear and unambiguous terms, is an express power given to the State Executives to fill casual vacancies in the Senate by temporary appointments. This does more than disprove the notion that the clause considered before could have been meant to give that power to the President of the United States. It shows that the notion, which lacks even the merit of being plausible, must have come from an intention to deceive the people that is too obvious to be hidden by sophistry and too outrageous to be excused by hypocrisy.

I have taken pains to choose this instance of misrepresentation and to set it in a clear and strong light, as unmistakable proof of the unwarrantable arts being practiced to prevent a fair and impartial judgment of the real merits of the Constitution now submitted to the people. In so flagrant a case, I have not hesitated to allow myself a severity of criticism that sits poorly with the general spirit of these papers. I am ready to submit to any fair and honest opponent of the proposed government the question whether language can supply any epithets too harsh for so shameless and so mercenary an attempt to impose on the citizens of America.
